TOP OF BOOK

  • UniCredit / Commerzbank (UCG / CBK) [DELTA ▲] — BaFin cleared UniCredit's application to cross 30% in CBK; file transferred to ECB for formal 60-working-day review. Simultaneously, CBK Q2 beat and Orlopp–Orcel direct talks confirmed.
    • Vs. baseline: UniCredit's application to hold more than 30% in Commerzbank cleared BaFin's completeness check in late July; BaFin subsequently referred the matter to the ECB for a formal assessment and final decision. The ECB has up to 60 working days to complete the review, potentially extendable by 20 days; if no suspensions, a decision is expected in the second half of October. On the earnings side, CBK posted Q2 net profit of €898 million (+94% YoY), beating consensus, and announced a €1.2bn buyback with CET1 remaining strong at 14.4%. CBK confirmed UniCredit has access to nearly 50% of voting rights and that talks on governance and cooperation are underway.
    • Read: The BaFin-to-ECB handoff is the structural inflection: regulatory binary now has a defined timeline (Oct). Once a buyer aims for more than 30%, prices start reflecting deal odds not just fundamentals — pulling CBK shares toward event-driven behaviour where approval headlines matter as much as loan growth. CBK's stated 100% payout ratio until CET1 reaches 13.5% and €3.2bn total 2026 distributions are a defensive floor against the deal uncertainty. CBK equity is event-driven from here; UCG equity faces binary on dilution from a deal vs. capital deployed in buybacks if it walks. AT1 and senior spreads on CBK should tighten on deal-premium expectations. Watch UCG RWA guidance if a full combination materialises. Action: Hold CBK equity as arb; monitor UCG AT1 for any deterioration in capital headroom as deal costs crystallise.
    • Sources: Bloomberg (BaFin nod), Bloomberg (CBK buyback/results), Wealth Briefing, Yahoo Finance (CBK call)
  • Fed / Macro Rates [DELTA ▼] — July 29 FOMC held 9-3; three hawkish dissents; most divided committee since 2016; rate-cut consensus for 2026 fully abandoned; September hike now a live risk.
    • Vs. baseline: The FOMC held at 3.50%–3.75% in a 9-3 vote, the most divided decision since 2016; by late July the rate-cut consensus that opened the year had fully reversed, and rate cuts are off the table at every major desk. All three dissents came from regional presidents — Hammack (Cleveland), Kashkari (Minneapolis), Logan (Dallas) — who voted to raise rates by 25bps at this meeting. US CPI for June fell to 3.5% YoY (vs 4.2% in May), with core easing to 2.6% — the first improvement in five months, driven by post-ceasefire energy relief. Jackson Hole (Aug 27-29) is the next signal event.
    • Read: Steepening risk at the front end: post-FOMC, the 10-year UST yield rose 5bps to 4.657% while the 30-year advanced more than 9bps to 5.193%. For European banks the transmission is: (1) rate-higher-for-longer in the US supports EUR NII hedging economics and widens the carry available on fixed-rate asset books; (2) simultaneously compresses cross-border M&A appetite and tightens leveraged-finance conditions — read-through negative for European CIB pipelines and USD funding costs for European bank branches. September FOMC (15-16 Sep) and Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote (Aug 28) are the next repricing events; Warsh stated his keynote is "a blank piece of paper right now," signalling no forward guidance commitment — data-dependency and volatility are the operative stance. Action: Keep duration short on senior non-preferred; monitor NII sensitivity guidance at Q3 calls.
    • Sources: CNBC (FOMC decision), BingX (FOMC analysis), Trading Economics (US CPI), Kansas City Fed (Jackson Hole)
  • ECB Rate Path [IN LINE] — July 23 hold at 2.25% confirmed; hawkish tone retained; September 10 meeting is live for another 25bp hike.
    • Vs. baseline: The ECB held rates unchanged at its July 23 meeting. Energy prices remain well above pre-conflict levels; the Governing Council stated uncertainty is high and that the full inflationary pass-through from the energy shock has not yet materialised. Lagarde stated explicitly that the hold should not be read as the end of the tightening cycle; with Brent above $95 at the time of the decision, the ECB's message was a tactical pause, not a pivot. The September 10 meeting is the next live window for a 25bp hike.
    • Read: For EU banks the transmission is asymmetric: a September hike extends NII tailwinds and delays deposit repricing pressure but compresses loan demand and raises funding costs on variable-rate liabilities. US CPI fell to 3.5% in June on post-ceasefire energy relief — the parallel disinflationary signal may give ECB hawks pause, but services inflation at ~3.5–4% is the ECB's primary concern and has not moved materially. Net: the September hike is a ~40–50% probability event, not a certainty. Action: Monitor the August CPI print (due ~mid-September) and Brent — the two variables that will decide the September call.
    • Sources: ECB press release (Jul 23), CFO Times

BY NAME / THEME

  • BNP Paribas (BNP) [DELTA ▲] — Q2 beat: revenue +12% (decade high), net profit +33%, CET1 13.0% hit 18 months ahead of target; interim dividend €3.23/share declared; accelerated distribution framework signalled.
    • Vs. baseline: Revenue up 12% to €12.2bn and net profit +33% to €3.0bn, including an €858m one-off capital gain from the Ageas/AGI transaction; management described these as the fastest top-line growth in a decade. Stripping the one-off, adjusted EPS grew 19%. CET1 reached 13.0% — the end-2027 target — 18 months early; CFO Machenil indicated a payout ratio of 70%+ is realistic from 2027; the board will consider distributing all excess capital above 13% annually, potentially starting with a special buyback alongside FY 2026 results. Cost of risk held at 39bps, within through-the-cycle guidance of <40bps.
    • Read: The capital overshoot is the key read-through for NII and spread durability: early CET1 target achievement reduces pressure to retain earnings, supporting higher distributions and tightening senior/AT1 spreads. Stock was unchanged at €140 post-results, suggesting the beat was priced or investors await distribution clarity. The real option is on the size of the Q4 buyback announcement. Key residual risk: Arval used-car residual value pressure expected to persist into H2, which could weigh on net interest margin in the consumer finance book. Equity — monitor for special buyback announcement at H2/FY26. Senior/AT1 — stable to positive on capital trajectory. Action: Hold equity; monitor Arval RV headwind vs. Global Markets sustainability.
    • Sources: BigGo Finance (BNP Q2 call), BNP Paribas IR
  • Deutsche Bank (DBK) [DELTA ▲] — Q2 / record H1: revenue +9% to €8.5bn (20th consecutive growth quarter), H1 PBT €5.7bn (+9%), NII guidance raised; first-ever buyback financed from current-year earnings (€500m).
    • Vs. baseline: Record H1 post-tax profit of €4.1bn (+11% YoY PBT), CET1 13.9%; management reaffirmed ~€33bn FY revenue ambition, raised NII guidance, and launched a new €500m buyback from 2026 earnings. NII €3.6bn in Q2; H1 credit loss provisions €979m, portfolio quality described as strong.
    • Read: The NII guidance raise is incrementally positive for net interest income trajectory, but rising provisions and US CRE exposure remain the key swing factor for forward earnings and credit spread widening risk. The first in-year buyback is a confidence signal from Sewing and a positioning move ahead of the CBK merger consolidation narrative — DBK is not in the deal but benefits from German banking consolidation premium. Equity — positive; Senior/AT1 stable. Action: Monitor Q3 CRE provision trajectory.
    • Sources: BigGo Finance (DBK Q2 call), Quartr (DBK summary)
  • National Bank of Greece (NBG / ETE) [DELTA ▲] — Q2 beat + guidance upgrade: H1 PAT €661m, NIM pivoted from Q1 trough, full-year ROTE/NII/EPS guidance all raised.
    • Vs. baseline: H1 profit €661m, ROTE 15.5% (over 20% adjusted for excess capital), NIM 273bps in Q2 — pivoting from Q1 lows, with NII +3% QoQ. CET1 17.3% post-payouts; full-year 2026 guidance upgraded: ROTE to >15%, NIM ~280bps, NII growth raised to mid-single-digits. Completed a €300m special buyback in H1; interim dividend intended for Q4.
    • Read: The NIM trough pivot is the most important transmission signal for Greek banking broadly — it eliminates a key bear case on NII compression heading into H2, and the QoQ NII recovery directly supports earnings visibility. With NPE ratio at 2.4% and CoR <40bps, asset quality is not yet a constraint. Senior spreads at 84bps as of mid-July (vs. 170bps in March 2024) — compression has been fast; less room left on credit leg. Equity: still constructive on loan growth and capital return optionality. Action: Monitor Q3 for NIM delivery at 280bps vs. ECB rate path.
    • Sources: GuruFocus (NBG call), Investing.com (NBG slides)
  • S&P Global (SPGI) [DELTA ▼] — Q2 EPS miss (~3-5% below consensus); Mobility spinoff creates optics noise; FY guidance cut at midpoint; stock -5% on day.
    • Vs. baseline: SPGI dropped over 5% after missing Q2 earnings estimates; annual adjusted EPS guidance reduced to a midpoint of $17.63, a 9.7% decrease, following the Mobility spinoff on July 1. Revenue of $4.15bn beat the street ($4.11bn expected), +10.4% YoY. CEO Cheung noted that the Iran conflict created complications for contract renewals in energy data, with the company extending deliberate pricing flexibility to affected customers.
    • Read: The guidance cut is partly mechanical (Mobility out) but the energy data segment weakness is a real delta — relevant for any name with CRE/energy data revenue. Ratings revenue +17% with private markets ratings +60%, helped by refinancing wall and M&A issuance — that is the strongest read-through for European leveraged finance: issuance activity is robust, which supports bank CIB fee lines, NII on underwriting exposures, and validates the direct-lending bifurcation thesis. Equity: SPGI's own stock is not a primary holding, but the Ratings data is. Action: Neutral on SPGI equity; read-through positive for EU bank CIB fee and private credit origination assumptions.
    • Sources: S&P Global IR, Blockonomi
  • Brent Crude / Middle East [DELTA ▲] — Brent ~$81/bbl on Aug 6 after Iran-Oman partial shipping agreement; UK Navy reported tanker explosions near Strait of Hormuz; US-Iran nuclear talks reportedly progressing but fragile.
    • Vs. baseline: Brent rose to ~$81/bbl on Aug 6 after Iran reached a provisional shipping agreement with Oman; Iranian and Omani officials stated the agreement falls short of full Hormuz reopening. US officials stated confidence that a broader deal was nearing. The UK Navy reported explosions near a tanker transiting the strait. Houthi forces — operating from Yemen and aligned with Iran — claimed attacks on a Saudi oil tanker and issued threats against additional vessels in the Red Sea. Price trajectory: peak crisis level ~$115 in late March; ceasefire-driven decline to ~$72 in June; current rebound to ~$81 on renewed incident risk.
    • Read: Oil in the $80–90 range corresponds to the ECB's "close to baseline" scenario from June projections — sustaining September hike optionality and supporting NII tailwinds for EU banks through higher-for-longer rates. A re-escalation above $95 reactivates the full-hike path, elevates provision expectations for energy-sector credit, and widens funding spreads for peripheral sovereigns. Read-through: energy companies' NII and fee contribution to universal bank P&Ls is elevated; E&P client hedging revenues supportive for FICC desks. Sovereign risk: periphery and EM oil importers face fiscal deterioration if Brent is sustained above $90, with negative read-through for sovereign spread widening and bank holdings of domestic government bonds. Action: Monitor Hormuz incident flow; flag if Brent breaks $90 as ECB September hike probability inflection.
    • Sources: Trading Economics (Brent)
  • European Private Credit (Sector) [IN LINE] — H1 2026 EMEA direct lending activity +4% YoY; bifurcation accelerating; "true" default rate closer to 5% when LMEs included; unitranche >47% of facilities.
    • Vs. baseline: Unitranche financing exceeded 47% of all European facilities in H1 2026; direct lending activity rose 4% YoY despite geopolitical and macro headwinds, with high-quality assets attracting significant investment while weaker credits face longer deal timelines and stricter diligence. High-profile leveraged loan defaults in late 2025 highlighted growing risks in the asset class; while the headline private credit default rate remained below 2%, once selective defaults and liability management exercises are included, the effective default rate approached 5% through the first nine months. The bifurcation between performing and distressed credits is widening funding spreads on weaker names and compressing them on top-tier borrowers, directly affecting the NII and fee income banks earn on their private credit co-investment and arranging books.
    • Read: The gap between headline and true default rates is the key risk for banks carrying private credit exposure on balance sheet or in CLO warehouses — mark-to-model assumptions on LME'd credits may not capture economic impairment, creating potential NII overstatement and future provision catch-up. Unitranche dominance reduces syndication fee revenue for arrangers but increases hold risk. Action: Monitor Q3 provision guidance from banks with direct lending JVs or significant leveraged finance warehouses; scrutinise LME disclosures.
    • Sources: Private Debt Investor (H1 2026 EMEA)
